Cowork 기능에 대한 전체 가이드는 Cowork 사용을 참조하세요.\n\n## 2026년 7월\n\n### 새로운 기능\n\n| 기능 | 설명 | 자세히 알아보기 |\n --- \n| 이벤트 기반 작업 | 일치하는 전자 메일 또는 Teams 메시지를 받을 때와 같이 문제가 발생할 때 실행되는 작업을 설정합니다(예: 인 경우 @mentioned)포함). 메시지에서 주의해야 할 사항을 설명하고, Cowork 검토하고 확인할 수 있는 자동화를 제안합니다. 이벤트 기반 작업은 예약 된 페이지의 예약된 프롬프트와 함께 표시됩니다. | 이벤트 기반 작업 설정 |\n\n## 2026년 6월(일반 공급)\n\n이제 모든 Microsoft 365 Copilot 테넌트에서 Cowork 일반 공급됩니다. 이 릴리스에서는 새 모델, 이미지 생성, 브라우저 사용, 사용자 지정 페이지 및 사용량 청구를 제공합니다.\n\n### 새로운 기능",

      "content": "Download your copy of Gartner, Innovation Insight: AI Middleware, Andrew Humphreys, Nicholas Carter, Keith Guttridge, 1 May 2026 →\n\nGartner is a trademark of Gartner, Inc. and/or its affiliates.\n\nAbout the author\n\nRahul Dureja   Chief Strategic Architect, Workato \n\nRahul Dureja has over 15 years of enterprise integration experience across TIBCO, MuleSoft, Oracle, and Salesforce. He helps organizations architect AI-ready orchestration platforms that transform fragile integrations into governed, enterprise-scale automation. Rahul specializes in bridging the gap between AI intelligence and reliable business execution.\n\n### Related Articles:\n\n- Agentic AI & MCP ## Why Philippine Enterprises Are Betting on Connectivity as Their AI Advantage [...] projects that the average Fortune 500 enterprise will run over 150,000 agents by 2028, up from fewer than 15 in 2025, and it recommends that organizations can use AI trust, risk, and security management (AI TRiSM) tools to help discover and categorize agents across applications, both from sanctioned tools, and from shadow AI solutions. Once organizations have an agent inventory, they can start to build adaptive controls to enforce the right policies based on the level of risk the agent presents. And we believe the June 2025 Gartner prediction that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by 2027 points to the same root cause: escalating costs, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls, the exact gaps AI middleware exists to close. [...] Where I’d push past the report is this: orchestration without governance is a gate with no fence, and governance without orchestration is a fence with nothing inside it. For MCP specifically, those two have to live on the same platform. That’s the layer we’re building at Workato, one execution architecture and one audit trail underneath every model and agent you run, with tool-level RBAC and an external MCP proxy still on our roadmap, not shipped today. In my opinion, the report’s conclusion stands regardless of vendor: AI middleware isn’t optional infrastructure anymore. It’s the thing that decides whether your AI investment scales or stalls.\n\nWant the full picture? The Gartner Innovation Insight report goes deeper into the capability map and the risks I’ve only summarized here.",

      "content": "“With the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence technology, we are extending our UKG Bryte Generative AI capabilities by developing AI agents that can understand and respond to customer needs in real-time, handling a broad array of tasks, from data analysis, to workflow automation, and customer support,” said Hugo Sarrazin, president, chief product and technology officer at UKG. “Our Bryte AI Agents will work alongside employees and managers, particularly those in frontline roles, taking on tasks that are best suited for technology.       "url": "https://www.ukg.com/company/newsroom/ukg-named-leader-hcm-twelfth-straight-year",

      "content": "Train Agents and Keep Them in the Loop \n\n  \n\nProblem: Without proper onboarding, agents either don’t trust the AI or trust it too much. \n\n  \n\nWhat to Do: \n\n Use real examples in training to show how AI supports decision-making but doesn’t replace human judgment.\n\n Emphasize the “human-in-the-loop” approach. It’s only as good as the data it’s working with.\n\n Make it easy for agents to flag issues or give feedback inside the workspace.\n\n Schedule regular check-ins to gather input, answer questions, and make improvements based on what is working. [...] Maintain consistency and quality via governance.\n\n Tag articles with clear metadata like topic and audience, so they’re easier for the AI to find and rank.\n\n Add summaries and section headings to improve readability for both agents and AI models.\n\n Assign owners to each knowledge article so there’s accountability for keeping content up to date.\n\n Create a regular process to review and improve knowledge content based on what agents need.\n\nExample: There are implementations that deliver weak search results and irrelevant agent recommendations due to inconsistent tagging. A targeted cleanup and retagging project led to a measurable improvement in response to relevance. \n\n  \n\nRoll Out Features Gradually and Plan for Growth [...] Continue to gather feedback and monitor usage analytics regularly to determine how users interact with the implemented AI features. Identify what’s working, what’s underused, and where users are struggling.\n\n Outdated or irrelevant articles reduce AI effectiveness. Set a recurring schedule to review and refresh knowledge base content. Encourage teams to contribute new articles, update existing ones, and share insights. Read More\n\n# Virtual Agent for HR Service Delivery\n\nAdi Subbarao\nServiceNow Employee\n\n## What is the ServiceNow Virtual Agent?\n\nServiceNow Virtual Agent is a chatbot solution native to the Now Platform which was recently launched during our London release. With Virtual Agent you can build conversational workflows for employees and customers to resolve common HR requests and inquiries via the chat interface of your choice.\n\nEnhance the Employee Experience using ServiceNow Virtual Agent\n\nWith Virtual Agent for HR Service Delivery, you can boost productivity across the entire HR department by: [...] ## How do you get started with Virtual Agent?\n\nVirtual Agent is available as part of the HR Professional & Enterprise Packages. Hospital revenue is the next version of that story. [...] — Dr. Martin Seneviratne, Co-CEO, R1 R37 AI Lab\n\nWhat makes R1’s position structurally different is the operational data underneath the AI. R1 annually processes 670 million patient encounters and 270 million payer transactions. Each customer’s dataset is used to fine-tune and continually enhance a system for that health system to predict denials before submission, route claims according to payer-specific rules, and learn from every interaction and decision. Every decision carries a full chain of reasoning visible to clinicians and compliance teams. [...] The patient rarely receives one bill; rather, they could receive several bills for the variety of services provided. The emergency physician group bills separately from the hospital.       "title": "AWS brings multi-agent orchestration to Bedrock | VentureBeat",
      "content": "“Using multi-agent collaboration in Amazon Bedrock, customers can get more accurate results by creating and assigning specialized agents for specific steps of a project and accelerate tasks by orchestrating multiple agents working in parallel,” AWS said.\n\nCustomers build their specialized agents on Bedrock, and then make a supervisor or orchestrator agent to help manage the other agents. AWS said the supervisor agent “handles the coordination, like breaking up and routing tasks to the right agents, giving specific agents access to the information they need to complete their work and determining what actions can be processed in parallel.” [...] AWS first introduced agentic capabilities in 2023 with the release of Agents on Bedrock, which offered enterprises a way to start building agents.       "title": "Deloitte Canada survey finds Canadian organizations are seeing AI returns, but may be measuring value too narrowly | Deloitte Canada",
      "content": "Support for AI sovereignty is also clear among Canadian leaders surveyed, with 96% saying it is important that AI technologies are developed, hosted, and governed under Canadian laws.\n\nData and systems remain key constraints to unlocking greater value\n\nAs organizations look to move beyond initial gains, data quality (59%) and legacy system integration (51%) remain the most commonly cited barriers. [...] While AI is now widely deployed, organizations may still be taking an incremental approach to how it is applied. Operations ranks as the top function for realized AI value today (57%), suggesting many organizations are focusing on improving existing processes rather than rethinking how work is done across the enterprise.\n\n\"Most leaders are still taking an incremental approach to AI because it's the path of least resistance,\" said Jas Jaaj, Global AI Markets, Ecosystems & Alliances Leader, Deloitte Canada. \"The step change comes when organizations expand their focus beyond efficiency and rethink how work gets done end-to-end.”\n\nConfidence in AI is high, but visibility across usage may be limited [...] “The leaders who are unlocking value aren’t waiting for perfect data,” said Dalmia. “They’re getting disciplined, focusing not just on individual use cases, but on the future of their businesses and individual functions with AI, as well as improving the data and systems that matter most for those priorities.       "url": "https://www.hrdive.com/spons/ai-isnt-hrs-biggest-challenge-confidence-is/826129",
      "title": "AI isn’t HR’s biggest challenge. Confidence is. | HR Dive",
      "content": "HR teams need room to experiment safely: a defined sandbox, low-risk tasks and clear ownership. Confidence is not built by another company-wide memo on AI governance. It is built through supervised practice.\n\nThis also means redefining success. The question is not whether AI can replace a process, but whether it can strip out the friction that stops HR people doing the work only they can do: coaching leaders, resolving complex employee issues and building trust. That is the real promise. Not automation for its own sake, but more capacity for the work that only people can do. [...] The same pattern holds across drafting employee communications, building interview guides, creating onboarding materials, summarizing policy updates and producing performance documentation. AI gets you from blank page to workable draft far quicker. That does not remove the need for HR expertise. It frees you to spend less time producing content and more time applying judgment. Judgment is still the differentiator. [...] #### Confidence.\n\nFor all the excitement around AI, many HR professionals are still unsure where it fits. Some worry about accuracy. Others question whether it belongs anywhere near sensitive employee matters. And there is the persistent fear that AI is quietly replacing the human element of HR. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also keeping teams from experiencing what AI does well.\n\nAnthropic recently published a survey of more than 50,000 Americans on their attitudes toward AI. One finding stood out: people who use AI every day at work are significantly less worried about losing their jobs to it than people who have never used it, 54 percent against 70 percent. That challenges the assumption that more exposure breeds more fear. The opposite appears to be true.",

      "url": "https://community.ibm.com/community/user/blogs/maryam-akmal/2025/11/08/ethical-ai-and-bias-mitigation-with-ibm-spss-a-com",
      "title": "Ethical AI and Bias Mitigation with IBM SPSS: A Comprehensive Framework for Responsible Analytics",
      "content": "#### By Maryam Akmal posted 11/08/25 08:12 AM\n\nAs AI and machine learning (ML) systems become more prevalent in decision-making across businesses, ethical concerns about algorithmic bias have grown. IBM SPSS, a statistical and predictive analytics pioneer, provides powerful solutions to handle these difficulties. This paper looks at how SPSS incorporates ethical AI concepts and bias mitigation measures, employing its sophisticated analytics capabilities to promote justice, transparency, and accountability. Using interdisciplinary research and real-world applications, we investigate the technological, sociological, and governance aspects of ethical AI within the SPSS ecosystem. [...] ### Data Preparation and Representation SPSS tools allow analysts to check data sets for representatives and balance. SPSS Modeller allows stratified sampling, which ensures proportional representation of demographic groupings. And to combat data shortage, SPSS incorporates synthetic data techniques, which reduces dependency on incomplete or skewed data sets. While in Feature Engineering, the analysts can omit proxy variables (such as zip codes) that are associated with protected attributes such as race. Meanwhile in a case study of bias mitigation strategies, a health-care study employing SPSS discovered biases in patient death forecasts skewed towards African-American groups. Reweighing training data and deleting racially linked variables increased the model's fairness by 32%. [...] ### Transparency and Explain-Ability SPSS emphasis interpret-ability as follows Explainable AI (XAI): The SPSS Visualization Designer provides intuitive charts to explain how variables influence predictions (for example, SHAP values in credit scoring). Audit Trails: All model iterations are kept, which allows regulators to trace decision rationale and identify bias sources.\n\n## Final Thoughts\n\nEthical AI is an ongoing process, not a checkbox. Organisations may reduce prejudice while realising the revolutionary promise of AI by using SPSS's technological rigour, governance tools, and dedication to fairness. According to Francesca Rossi, IBM's Chief AI Ethics Officer, \"The goal is not just to avoid harm but to actively promote equity\".\n\n## Permalink\n\nCopy\n\n## \n\n#### Office",

      "url": "https://www.shrm.org/foundation/skills-first-future/resource-library/employer-example-workday",
      "title": "Employer Example: Workday",
      "content": "Header Image\nHeader Image 2\n\n## EMPLOYER EXAMPLE: Workday\n\nWorkday’s skills-first transformation shows how HR leaders can drive better hiring, retention, and development by aligning talent practices with business needs and quality data.\n\nEMPLOYER EXAMPLE: Workday\n\n### INTRODUCTION\n\nWorkday is the enterprise AI platform for managing people, money, and agents. With nearly 21,000 employees worldwide, Workday sits at a unique intersection: the same talent challenges its platform is designed to help customers solve are ones the company faces internally. In 2021, Workday's leadership made a deliberate decision to put that to the test — building a skills-first organization from the inside out. [...] Learning alignment addressed the gap between content availability and relevance. Once Workday identified critical skills for every job, it mapped those skills to existing learning content. Content purchasing decisions were restructured so that every employee now has access to development resources focused on the skills that matter most to their role.\n\nPerformance and career development integration brought skills into the review process itself. As part of performance conversations, employees identify one critical skill to focus on over the next three to six months, align on that choice with their manager, and receive AI-driven learning recommendations in Career Hub tied directly to that development goal. [...] On the demand side, the organization undertook a rigorous process to identify the 10 to 12 most critical skills for every role. The team drew on internal data — job descriptions, requisitions, worker profiles, and career pathing history — and partnered with an external skills data company to layer in market intelligence. Managers were surveyed to rate the importance of candidate skills to performance in their specific roles. Senior leaders then reviewed those results and made the final selections. Now, every job at Workday has a defined set of job-critical skills attached to it, giving HR a consistent and credible foundation for every practice that follows.",

The audit must assess how the cyber program safeguards personal information from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure, as well as unauthorized activity resulting in the loss of availability of personal information. It must also assess how the company established, implemented, and maintains its program (including the written policies and procedures), and how the company enforces compliance.\n\nThe rule includes a long list of program components subject to the audit. Examples include:\n\nFor each component, the audit must describe its effectiveness in safeguarding personal information, describe any gaps or weaknesses, and document the company’s plan to address those gaps or weaknesses. [...] Article 9 establishes a cybersecurity audit requirement designed to confirm that organizations processing significant amounts of personal information maintain cybersecurity programs capable of safeguarding that information from security threats. While 88% of leaders are confident they can measure AI return on investment and 90% report positive productivity impacts over the past 12 months, the most common indicators of ROI remain productivity gains and cost savings. Fewer leaders point to broader business outcomes such as revenue growth or risk reduction, suggesting many organizations may be capturing AI’s most immediate benefits without yet unlocking its full strategic value.       "url": "https://www.hrdive.com/spons/ai-isnt-hrs-biggest-challenge-confidence-is/826129",
      "title": "AI isn't HR's biggest challenge. Confidence is.",
      "content": "#### Confidence.\n\nFor all the excitement around AI, many HR professionals are still unsure where it fits. Some worry about accuracy. Others question whether it belongs anywhere near sensitive employee matters. And there is the persistent fear that AI is quietly replacing the human element of HR. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also keeping teams from experiencing what AI does well.\n\nAnthropic recently published a survey of more than 50,000 Americans on their attitudes toward AI. One finding stood out: people who use AI every day at work are significantly less worried about losing their jobs to it than people who have never used it, 54 percent against 70 percent. That challenges the assumption that more exposure breeds more fear. The opposite appears to be true. [...] The same pattern holds across drafting employee communications, building interview guides, creating onboarding materials, summarizing policy updates and producing performance documentation. AI gets you from blank page to workable draft far quicker. That does not remove the need for HR expertise. It frees you to spend less time producing content and more time applying judgment. Judgment is still the differentiator. [...] “I saw this recently with an HR team we were supporting. They were drowning in a recurring documentation task, think offer letters. Rather than buy a new platform, we built two AI agents within the customer's existing Microsoft environment to keep data secure. The first drafted from a locked template; the second checked that draft against a fixed set of criteria; and a person reviewed every output before it went anywhere. Work that once took most of a day now takes under 30 minutes, with higher quality because HR reviews and refines rather than starts from scratch. It also freed enough time to help that team stand up a leadership programme they simply could not have run before, because the administrative burden had always been in the way.”",

      "title": "Sana AI Agents from Workday | Workday IN",
      "content": "## FAQs.\n\n## FAQs.\n\n### What are Sana AI agents?\n\nAI agents are systems that can understand details across contexts, reason through situations, plan toward a goal, take autonomous action within human-defined parameters, and learn from experience. With Sana from Workday, AI agents can be built directly into Workday to automate processes and enable new AI-driven business workflows.\n\n### How do AI agents differ from traditional chatbots?\n\nChatbots don’t “think”—they rely on pre-programmed logic, respond only when prompted by a user, and can’t learn from experience or adapt to unfamiliar situations.\n\n### Can AI agents take actions on behalf of employees or managers? [...] Our AI agents are designed to augment human workers, not replace them. We take responsible AI seriously, holding ISO 42001 accreditation and independent attestation of alignment with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The primary goal of Workday agents is to free your people to focus on higher-value work, such as strategic analysis and complex problem-solving, where human skills are most impactful.\n\n### Are AI agents available out of the box in Workday or fully customizable?\n\nSana agents are broad in scope and supported by dedicated engineering teams, a product roadmap, and multiple agent skills.       "url": "https://www.shrm.org/foundation/skills-first-future/resource-library/employer-example-workday",
      "title": "Employer Example: Workday",
      "content": "Header Image\nHeader Image 2\n\n## EMPLOYER EXAMPLE: Workday\n\nWorkday’s skills-first transformation shows how HR leaders can drive better hiring, retention, and development by aligning talent practices with business needs and quality data.\n\nEMPLOYER EXAMPLE: Workday\n\n### INTRODUCTION\n\nWorkday is the enterprise AI platform for managing people, money, and agents. With nearly 21,000 employees worldwide, Workday sits at a unique intersection: the same talent challenges its platform is designed to help customers solve are ones the company faces internally. In 2021, Workday's leadership made a deliberate decision to put that to the test — building a skills-first organization from the inside out. [...] Learning alignment addressed the gap between content availability and relevance. Once Workday identified critical skills for every job, it mapped those skills to existing learning content. Content purchasing decisions were restructured so that every employee now has access to development resources focused on the skills that matter most to their role.\n\nPerformance and career development integration brought skills into the review process itself. As part of performance conversations, employees identify one critical skill to focus on over the next three to six months, align on that choice with their manager, and receive AI-driven learning recommendations in Career Hub tied directly to that development goal. [...] On the demand side, the organization undertook a rigorous process to identify the 10 to 12 most critical skills for every role. The team drew on internal data — job descriptions, requisitions, worker profiles, and career pathing history — and partnered with an external skills data company to layer in market intelligence. Managers were surveyed to rate the importance of candidate skills to performance in their specific roles. Senior leaders then reviewed those results and made the final selections. Now, every job at Workday has a defined set of job-critical skills attached to it, giving HR a consistent and credible foundation for every practice that follows.",

      "url": "https://www.workato.com/the-connector/what-is-ai-middleware",
      "title": "What is AI middleware?",
      "content": "Where I’d push past the report is this: orchestration without governance is a gate with no fence, and governance without orchestration is a fence with nothing inside it. For MCP specifically, those two have to live on the same platform. That’s the layer we’re building at Workato, one execution architecture and one audit trail underneath every model and agent you run, with tool-level RBAC and an external MCP proxy still on our roadmap, not shipped today.       "content": "대한민국 (한국어)\n\n# Workday, 에이전트 시대에 필요한 인재 확보 솔루션\n\nWorkday가 2026년 인재 확보 솔루션 가트너® 매직 쿼드런트™에서 리더 그룹에 선정되었습니다. 각 조직에서 AI 기반 에이전트를 활용해 채용 속도를 높이고, 후보자 경험을 개선하고, 채용의 규모를 확장하도록 꾸준히 지원해 온 점을 높이 평가받은 것입니다.\n\nWorkday가 2026년 인재 확보 솔루션 가트너® 매직 쿼드런트™에서 리더 그룹에 선정되었습니다. 각 조직에서 AI 기반 에이전트를 활용해 채용 속도를 높이고, 후보자 경험을 개선하고, 채용의 규모를 확장하도록 꾸준히 지원해 온 점을 높이 평가받은 것입니다.\n\n최신 소식\n\n사무실 안에서 컴퓨터를 보고 있는 세 사람\n\n## 업무 환경의 신기원을 열 차세대 Agentic AI를 내놓은 Workday\n\nHR팀, 재무팀, IT팀, 법무팀 모두 수백 가지의 새로운 AI 기능과 에이전트를 활용해 번거롭고 반복적인 일에서 벗어나 진정으로 중요한 임무에 집중할 수 있습니다.\n\nHR팀, 재무팀, IT팀, 법무팀 모두 수백 가지의 새로운 AI 기능과 에이전트를 활용해 번거롭고 반복적인 일에서 벗어나 진정으로 중요한 임무에 집중할 수 있습니다.\n\n## 2026년 세계에서 가장 윤리적인 기업에 선정된 Workday\n\nWorkday의 최고법률책임자(CLO)이자 대외 협력 부문 책임자인 Rich Sauer와 함께 이번 수상의 의미, 그리고 Workday가 실무 현장에서 윤리와 청렴을 실천하는 방식을 짚어 봤습니다.       "title": "Deloitte Canada survey finds Canadian organizations are ...",
      "content": "While AI is now widely deployed, organizations may still be taking an incremental approach to how it is applied. Operations ranks as the top function for realized AI value today (57%), suggesting many organizations are focusing on improving existing processes rather than rethinking how work is done across the enterprise.\n\n\"Most leaders are still taking an incremental approach to AI because it's the path of least resistance,\" said Jas Jaaj, Global AI Markets, Ecosystems & Alliances Leader, Deloitte Canada. \"The step change comes when organizations expand their focus beyond efficiency and rethink how work gets done end-to-end.”\n\nConfidence in AI is high, but visibility across usage may be limited [...] Toronto, July 28, 2026 — A new Deloitte Canada survey of senior leaders finds Canadian organizations are seeing measurable returns from AI, but many may be limiting its long-term impact by focusing on the most visible gains rather than broader measures of business value. While 88% of leaders are confident they can measure AI return on investment and 90% report positive productivity impacts over the past 12 months, the most common indicators of ROI remain productivity gains and cost savings. Fewer leaders point to broader business outcomes such as revenue growth or risk reduction, suggesting many organizations may be capturing AI’s most immediate benefits without yet unlocking its full strategic value. [...] Support for AI sovereignty is also clear among Canadian leaders surveyed, with 96% saying it is important that AI technologies are developed, hosted, and governed under Canadian laws.\n\nData and systems remain key constraints to unlocking greater value\n\nAs organizations look to move beyond initial gains, data quality (59%) and legacy system integration (51%) remain the most commonly cited barriers. At the same time, better data (45%) is seen as the single biggest accelerator of stronger outcomes.\n\nLeaders are continuing to invest, with 86% planning to increase AI upskilling, and 92% reporting that employees view AI’s impact positively.",

    {
      "url": "https://www.hrdive.com/spons/ai-isnt-hrs-biggest-challenge-confidence-is/826129",
      "title": "AI isn't HR's biggest challenge. Confidence is.",
      "content": "#### Confidence.\n\nFor all the excitement around AI, many HR professionals are still unsure where it fits. Some worry about accuracy. Others question whether it belongs anywhere near sensitive employee matters. And there is the persistent fear that AI is quietly replacing the human element of HR. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also keeping teams from experiencing what AI does well.\n\nAnthropic recently published a survey of more than 50,000 Americans on their attitudes toward AI. One finding stood out: people who use AI every day at work are significantly less worried about losing their jobs to it than people who have never used it, 54 percent against 70 percent. That challenges the assumption that more exposure breeds more fear. The opposite appears to be true. [...] The same pattern holds across drafting employee communications, building interview guides, creating onboarding materials, summarizing policy updates and producing performance documentation. AI gets you from blank page to workable draft far quicker. That does not remove the need for HR expertise. It frees you to spend less time producing content and more time applying judgment. Judgment is still the differentiator. [...] “I saw this recently with an HR team we were supporting. They were drowning in a recurring documentation task, think offer letters. Rather than buy a new platform, we built two AI agents within the customer's existing Microsoft environment to keep data secure. The first drafted from a locked template; the second checked that draft against a fixed set of criteria; and a person reviewed every output before it went anywhere. Work that once took most of a day now takes under 30 minutes, with higher quality because HR reviews and refines rather than starts from scratch. It also freed enough time to help that team stand up a leadership programme they simply could not have run before, because the administrative burden had always been in the way.”",
      "score": 0.19273713,
      "raw_content": null
    },

      "url": "https://kpmg.com/cy/en/insights/transformation/transforming-the-enterprise.html",
      "title": "Transforming the Enterprise",
      "content": "This is not simply a transformation challenge. It is a leadership challenge.\n\nBased on a global survey of 1,750 senior transformation leaders across 20 countries, as well as perspectives from KPMG alliance organizations including ServiceNow, Workday, SAP, and Oracle, Transforming the Enterprise 2026 explores a critical shift. It examines why traditional coordination models are breaking down and why enterprise orchestration is becoming the defining capability for sustained performance in the enterprise of the future.\n\n## Key findings\n\n### Enterprise performance is not keeping pace [...] As intelligence becomes embedded across decision-making, operations, customer experiences, and workflows, enterprise transformation is no longer occurring through isolated initiatives. Change is unfolding continuously across the enterprise, creating a level of complexity most organizations were never designed to absorb. Organizations are now managing an average of 3.5 transformation initiatives concurrently, often spanning multiple functions and operating environments at once.\n\nWhat was once episodic has become continuous. The pressure to align priorities, coordinate execution, and sustain performance is increasing as transformation accelerates.\n\nMost organizations, however, are accelerating transformation faster than they are redesigning the enterprise to sustain it. [...] AI is accelerating productivity and experimentation, but many organizations are layering AI onto fragmented workflows and disconnected systems. Sustained value depends on redesigning work, decision-making, and execution across the enterprise, supported by stronger enterprise AI strategy, enterprise AI governance, and enterprise trust.\n\n### Enterprise orchestration is becoming the defining leadership capability\n\nOrganizations pulling ahead are not necessarily transforming more than their peers. They are better able to align priorities, integrate execution, and direct transformation coherently across interconnected systems, workflows, and decisions.\n\n## Three priorities for orchestrating enterprise transformation\n\n###### Rebuild the foundations",

      "url": "https://www.shrm.org/foundation/skills-first-future/resource-library/employer-example-workday",
      "title": "Employer Example: Workday",
      "content": "Header Image\nHeader Image 2\n\n## EMPLOYER EXAMPLE: Workday\n\nWorkday’s skills-first transformation shows how HR leaders can drive better hiring, retention, and development by aligning talent practices with business needs and quality data.\n\nEMPLOYER EXAMPLE: Workday\n\n### INTRODUCTION\n\nWorkday is the enterprise AI platform for managing people, money, and agents. With nearly 21,000 employees worldwide, Workday sits at a unique intersection: the same talent challenges its platform is designed to help customers solve are ones the company faces internally. In 2021, Workday's leadership made a deliberate decision to put that to the test — building a skills-first organization from the inside out. [...] Learning alignment addressed the gap between content availability and relevance. Once Workday identified critical skills for every job, it mapped those skills to existing learning content. Content purchasing decisions were restructured so that every employee now has access to development resources focused on the skills that matter most to their role.\n\nPerformance and career development integration brought skills into the review process itself. As part of performance conversations, employees identify one critical skill to focus on over the next three to six months, align on that choice with their manager, and receive AI-driven learning recommendations in Career Hub tied directly to that development goal. [...] On the demand side, the organization undertook a rigorous process to identify the 10 to 12 most critical skills for every role. The team drew on internal data — job descriptions, requisitions, worker profiles, and career pathing history — and partnered with an external skills data company to layer in market intelligence. Managers were surveyed to rate the importance of candidate skills to performance in their specific roles. Senior leaders then reviewed those results and made the final selections. Now, every job at Workday has a defined set of job-critical skills attached to it, giving HR a consistent and credible foundation for every practice that follows.",

      "url": "https://www.hrdive.com/spons/ai-isnt-hrs-biggest-challenge-confidence-is/826129",
      "title": "AI isn't HR's biggest challenge. Confidence is.",
      "content": "#### Confidence.\n\nFor all the excitement around AI, many HR professionals are still unsure where it fits. Some worry about accuracy. Others question whether it belongs anywhere near sensitive employee matters. And there is the persistent fear that AI is quietly replacing the human element of HR. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also keeping teams from experiencing what AI does well.\n\nAnthropic recently published a survey of more than 50,000 Americans on their attitudes toward AI. One finding stood out: people who use AI every day at work are significantly less worried about losing their jobs to it than people who have never used it, 54 percent against 70 percent. That challenges the assumption that more exposure breeds more fear. The opposite appears to be true. [...] The same pattern holds across drafting employee communications, building interview guides, creating onboarding materials, summarizing policy updates and producing performance documentation. AI gets you from blank page to workable draft far quicker. That does not remove the need for HR expertise. It frees you to spend less time producing content and more time applying judgment. Judgment is still the differentiator. [...] “I saw this recently with an HR team we were supporting. They were drowning in a recurring documentation task, think offer letters. Rather than buy a new platform, we built two AI agents within the customer's existing Microsoft environment to keep data secure. The first drafted from a locked template; the second checked that draft against a fixed set of criteria; and a person reviewed every output before it went anywhere. Work that once took most of a day now takes under 30 minutes, with higher quality because HR reviews and refines rather than starts from scratch. It also freed enough time to help that team stand up a leadership programme they simply could not have run before, because the administrative burden had always been in the way.”",
      "score": 0.19273713,
      "raw_content": null
    },

      "content": "Where I’d push past the report is this: orchestration without governance is a gate with no fence, and governance without orchestration is a fence with nothing inside it. In my opinion, the report’s conclusion stands regardless of vendor: AI middleware isn’t optional infrastructure anymore. It’s the thing that decides whether your AI investment scales or stalls.\n\nWant the full picture?       "url": "https://www.hrdive.com/spons/ai-isnt-hrs-biggest-challenge-confidence-is/826129",
      "title": "AI isn't HR's biggest challenge. Confidence is.",
      "content": "#### Confidence.\n\nFor all the excitement around AI, many HR professionals are still unsure where it fits. Some worry about accuracy. Others question whether it belongs anywhere near sensitive employee matters. And there is the persistent fear that AI is quietly replacing the human element of HR. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also keeping teams from experiencing what AI does well.\n\nAnthropic recently published a survey of more than 50,000 Americans on their attitudes toward AI. One finding stood out: people who use AI every day at work are significantly less worried about losing their jobs to it than people who have never used it, 54 percent against 70 percent. That challenges the assumption that more exposure breeds more fear. The opposite appears to be true. [...] The same pattern holds across drafting employee communications, building interview guides, creating onboarding materials, summarizing policy updates and producing performance documentation. AI gets you from blank page to workable draft far quicker. That does not remove the need for HR expertise. It frees you to spend less time producing content and more time applying judgment. Judgment is still the differentiator. [...] “I saw this recently with an HR team we were supporting. They were drowning in a recurring documentation task, think offer letters. Rather than buy a new platform, we built two AI agents within the customer's existing Microsoft environment to keep data secure. The first drafted from a locked template; the second checked that draft against a fixed set of criteria; and a person reviewed every output before it went anywhere. Work that once took most of a day now takes under 30 minutes, with higher quality because HR reviews and refines rather than starts from scratch. It also freed enough time to help that team stand up a leadership programme they simply could not have run before, because the administrative burden had always been in the way.”",

      "title": "Deloitte Canada survey finds Canadian organizations are ...",
      "content": "While AI is now widely deployed, organizations may still be taking an incremental approach to how it is applied. Operations ranks as the top function for realized AI value today (57%), suggesting many organizations are focusing on improving existing processes rather than rethinking how work is done across the enterprise.\n\n\"Most leaders are still taking an incremental approach to AI because it's the path of least resistance,\" said Jas Jaaj, Global AI Markets, Ecosystems & Alliances Leader, Deloitte Canada. \"The step change comes when organizations expand their focus beyond efficiency and rethink how work gets done end-to-end.”\n\nConfidence in AI is high, but visibility across usage may be limited [...] Toronto, July 28, 2026 — A new Deloitte Canada survey of senior leaders finds Canadian organizations are seeing measurable returns from AI, but many may be limiting its long-term impact by focusing on the most visible gains rather than broader measures of business value. While 88% of leaders are confident they can measure AI return on investment and 90% report positive productivity impacts over the past 12 months, the most common indicators of ROI remain productivity gains and cost savings. Fewer leaders point to broader business outcomes such as revenue growth or risk reduction, suggesting many organizations may be capturing AI’s most immediate benefits without yet unlocking its full strategic value. [...] \"Most organizations are still measuring the easiest value, not the most important value,\" said Nihar Dalmia, Partner in AI & Data, Deloitte Canada. \"Productivity and cost savings matter, but they are only the first layer.       "url": "https://www.hrdive.com/spons/ai-isnt-hrs-biggest-challenge-confidence-is/826129",
      "title": "AI isn't HR's biggest challenge. Confidence is.",
      "content": "#### Confidence.\n\nFor all the excitement around AI, many HR professionals are still unsure where it fits. Some worry about accuracy. Others question whether it belongs anywhere near sensitive employee matters. And there is the persistent fear that AI is quietly replacing the human element of HR. Those concerns are understandable, but they are also keeping teams from experiencing what AI does well.\n\nAnthropic recently published a survey of more than 50,000 Americans on their attitudes toward AI. One finding stood out: people who use AI every day at work are significantly less worried about losing their jobs to it than people who have never used it, 54 percent against 70 percent. That challenges the assumption that more exposure breeds more fear. The opposite appears to be true. [...] The same pattern holds across drafting employee communications, building interview guides, creating onboarding materials, summarizing policy updates and producing performance documentation. AI gets you from blank page to workable draft far quicker. That does not remove the need for HR expertise. It frees you to spend less time producing content and more time applying judgment. Judgment is still the differentiator. [...] “I saw this recently with an HR team we were supporting. They were drowning in a recurring documentation task, think offer letters. Rather than buy a new platform, we built two AI agents within the customer's existing Microsoft environment to keep data secure. The first drafted from a locked template; the second checked that draft against a fixed set of criteria; and a person reviewed every output before it went anywhere. Work that once took most of a day now takes under 30 minutes, with higher quality because HR reviews and refines rather than starts from scratch. It also freed enough time to help that team stand up a leadership programme they simply could not have run before, because the administrative burden had always been in the way.”",

      "content": "### Evaluating Agentic Workflows Against Human Baselines\n\nTreasury teams are testing AI agents for cash management tasks such as forecasting short-term liquidity needs and recommending intercompany transfers.\n\nAI plays a role in the on-chain economy as agentic workflows extend into digital asset settlement.\n\nBefore scaling an AI agent beyond a pilot, finance teams benchmark its decision-making accuracy against a human baseline over a defined evaluation period.\n\n### The agentic AI playbook for the enterprise\n\nai\nai\n\n## Designing an AI System for Finance\n\n### Specifying KPIs and Data Requirements\n\nAI system design in finance starts with the business metric the system must move, whether that is fraud losses avoided, processing time reduced, or forecast accuracy improved.       "url": "https://www.bettercloud.com/monitor/agentic-ai-is-the-next-layer-of-it-automation",
      "title": "Agentic AI is emerging as the next layer of IT automation | BetterCloud",
      "content": "An agent that can execute a workflow at 2am, without a human in the loop, can also execute the wrong workflow at 2am with nobody watching.\n\nWe’ve spent decades building IT operations around the assumption that a person initiates the action and is accountable for it. Agentic AI breaks that assumption. The action still needs to happen. The accountability still needs to exist. But the initiator is no longer a person sitting at a keyboard.\n\nThis is why AI governance for IT automation has to be treated as a foundational requirement, not an afterthought bolted on after agents are already running in production. Every organization deploying agentic AI needs clear answers to a few non-negotiable questions: [...] Think about what this looks like in practice across a modern SaaS environment. Instead of an IT admin building an automation rule to offboard a departing employee, an agent notices the HR system update, cross-references app ownership and license data, initiates deprovisioning, and reassigns files, all without a ticket ever being filed. Instead of a security team manually reviewing access requests, an agent evaluates the request against policy, approves or escalates it, and logs the decision for audit.\n\nThis is what we mean when we talk about AI agents managing SaaS workflows. Not a chatbot embedded in a helpdesk tool. A system with the context, permissions, and initiative to run parts of IT operations on its own.\n\n## Why this is happening now [...] We built our Access and AI Control Layer with exactly this shift in mind, because non-human identities and agentic AI are quickly becoming as common in the SaaS environment as human users, and they need the same rigor around access, activity, and control that we’ve always applied to people.\n\n## Where this goes from here\n\nAgentic AI in IT operations isn’t a future state. It’s already showing up in provisioning, offboarding, access reviews, and workflow orchestration inside organizations today, often faster than the governance frameworks meant to contain it.\n\nThe IT leaders who get ahead of this won’t be the ones who avoid agentic AI. They’ll be the ones who put the right execution and governance layer underneath it before it scales past their ability to control it.",

    {
      "url": "https://www.ey.com/en_in/media/podcasts/ai/2026/07/episode-32-why-strong-governance-is-important-to-scale-agentic-ai",
      "title": "Why strong governance is important to scale Agentic AI | EY - India",
      "content": "The first thing organizations need to accept is that an AI agent can be given authority, but it cannot be given accountability. Accountability will still sit with the enterprise. So, every agent needs clear ownership. Who owns the business process? Who owns the technology and who owns the risk? Human supervision also needs to be more thoughtful. It should not just be a checkbox where we simply say a human is somewhere in the loop.  \n    \n For low-risk tasks, monitoring and exception reporting may suffice, but if the agent is taking actions that affect money, customers, compliance or reputation, then there should be adequate approval gates that are built in escalation, parts that are clearly defined, and a very clear and precise way to pause or reverse what the agent is doing. [...] #### Aditya\n\nAgentic AI is not just another technology rollout or a standard technology rollout. It changes how work actually gets done. If an agent can plan a task, update a record, trigger workflows, or coordinate across systems in the enterprise, then it is effectively becoming part of the operating model itself. That means that organizations have to rethink roles, approvals, controls, SOPs, as well as escalation parts.  \n    \n They also need to decide what stays human-led, what becomes agent-assisted, and what can be fully agent-executed. In many cases, the hard part will not be building the agent but  redesigning the way people, processes and controls work around it.  \n\n#### Pallavi [...] ### Key takeaways:\n\n Agentic AI can act autonomously, but accountability must always remain with the enterprise.\n Effective governance requires continuous monitoring, strong guardrails, audit trails and clear ownership.\n Successful AI scaling depends on operating model redesign, and not just technology implementation.\n It is important to treat AI agents as non-human identities with strictly controlled, least-privilege access.\n Enterprises should implement safeguards against AI-related risks such as prompt injection, misuse of tools, unauthorized actions and data leakage.\n\n> Agentic AI is not just transforming technology; it is reshaping how work gets done, requiring organizations to rethink roles, controls and governance.\n\nAditya Iyer\n\nPartner, Risk Consulting, EY India\n\n### Speaker",

      "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/admin/manage/get-started-frontier?view=o365-worldwide",
      "title": "Get started with the Microsoft Copilot Frontier Program - Microsoft 365 admin | Microsoft Learn",
      "content": "# Get started with the Microsoft Copilot Frontier Program\n\nThe Microsoft Frontier program gives organizations early access to innovative and emerging AI capabilities in Microsoft 365 before those features reach general availability (GA). By opting in to Frontier, IT administrators can evaluate new Microsoft Copilot agents and AI-powered experiences, determine readiness for broader deployment across their tenant, and provide feedback about Frontier feature capabilities to Microsoft.\n\nImportant\n\nFrontier is managed at the tenant level. Production tenants can safely enroll users into the Frontier program to allow your organization access to Frontier features. IT admins have explicit control which users have access to which Frontier features. [...] To turn on Frontier preview experiences for your users, do the following steps:\n\n1. Sign in to the Microsoft 365 admin center.\n2. Go to Copilot > Settings.\n3. Select the View all tab.\n4. In the Search all Copilot settings search bar, type \"Frontier\".\n5. Select Copilot Frontier.\n6. Choose how Frontier access is assigned in your organization:\n\n    No access (default)\n    All users\n    Specific users\n\nAfter you turn on Frontier experiences for your organization, eligible users can access supported preview features as they're released. It might take three hours for Frontier features and agents to be available to users.\n\nNote [...] ### Deploy agents to your users directly\n\nYou can install and pin specific agents to select users or groups directly rather than users needing to search the Agent store. This method helps users start using Frontier agents more quickly.\n\n1. Go to Agents > All agents.\n2. Select the agent you want to install.\n3. In the Users tab, add the specific users or security groups that you want to use this agent.\n    Use a Microsoft Entra ID security group to target specific users who can access Frontier agents. This approach helps you validate experiences with a small group before broad rollout.\n4. In the agent flyout, select Install. To help users find the agent, you can select Pin for users. The agent appears in the Microsoft 365 Copilot app.\n\n### Manage AI provider large language models",

      "url": "https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoft-security-blog/securing-ai-agents-at-runtime-real-time-protection-and-threat-detection-for-micr/4541255",
      "title": "Securing AI Agents at Runtime: Real-Time Protection and Threat Detection for Microsoft Agent 365 | Microsoft Community Hub",
      "content": "## Threat detection for Microsoft Agent 365 Agents (Public Preview)\n\nThreat detection provides SOC teams with detailed visibility into attacks and suspicious activity targeting AI agents. By analyzing runtime signals across agent interactions, tool usage, and execution patterns, Microsoft Defender identifies suspicious and malicious behavior throughout the agent execution lifecycle and surfaces actionable security alerts for SOC teams. \n\nThreat detection supports cloud agent types that emit observability logs to Microsoft Agent 365, including: \n\n Microsoft Copilot Studio\n\n Microsoft Foundry\n\n Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder\n\n Agents integrated through the Microsoft Agent 365 SDK [...] Agents integrated through the Microsoft Agent 365 SDK\n\nThis provides consistent threat visibility across supported Microsoft Agent 365 agent experiences, regardless of how the agent was built. \n\n                  Fig. 1. Microsoft Security for AI alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR (Preview) \n\nMicrosoft Defender identifies a broad range of AI-specific threats, including: \n\n Indirect prompt injection (XPIA)— malicious instructions embedded in external content designed to manipulate agent behavior.\n\n Evasion techniques— attempts to bypass agent instructions or security controls.\n\n Malicious content propagation — attempts to use agents to generate or distribute malicious content.\n\n Secret leakage — exposure of credentials, API keys, or other sensitive information through agent interactions. [...] LLM reconnaissance — attempts to probe agent capabilities, instructions, or security boundaries.\n\n Suspicious IP access — agent access originating from anonymized or suspicious IP addresses.\n\nAlerts are surfaced directly in Microsoft Defender, enabling SOC analysts to investigate and respond using familiar workflows, Advanced Hunting queries, and the Defender XDR investigation experience. \n\n## Real-time protection for WorkIQ and Custom MCP servers (General Availability)\n\nReal-time protection moves beyond detection by blocking threats inline when AI agents interact with WorkIQ and custom MCP servers (see Microsoft Agent 365 tooling servers).",

      "content": "## Forum Discussion\n\nDavidEnestvedt's avatar\n\nDavidEnestvedt\n\nOccasional Reader\n\nJul 27, 2026\n\n# Is \"Popular in Your Org\" in the Agent Store Actually Based on Usage?\n\nI've noticed something interesting in the Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Store and I'm curious if others are seeing the same behavior.\n\nIn the \"Popular in Your Org\" section, many of the agents being surfaced are either:\n\n Blocked by our administrators\n Not available for me to install\n Restricted due to licensing or governance settings\n\nThis creates a somewhat confusing experience because the label implies these are agents that are actively being used or adopted within my organization. However, if users cannot install or access them, it raises questions about what \"Popular in Your Org\" actually means. [...] Otherwise, it feels a bit misleading to highlight agents that users discover but ultimately cannot access.\n\nWould love to hear whether others have had the same experience and whether Microsoft has shared any guidance on how this section is populated.\n\nThanks!\n\ncopilot chat\n\nmicrosoft 365 copilot\n\ntraining and resources",

      "url": "https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/telecommunications-industry-blog/building-autonomous-network-operations-from-vision-to-measurable-business-impact/4540483",
      "title": "Building Autonomous Network Operations: From Vision to ...",
      "content": "#### The Road Ahead\n\nLooking forward, both leaders expect the next wave of innovation to come from expanding agentic workflows across the enterprise. Austin described applying agents beyond network operations into functions such as finance, HR, and broader business operations. Gaudette emphasized the growing importance of knowledge systems and skills frameworks that allow agents to collaborate across organizational boundaries and optimize end-to-end processes.\n\nThe message from DTW Ignite 2026 was clear: autonomous networks are no longer defined by experimentation. The leaders who are creating competitive advantage are those connecting AI directly to operational outcomes. [...] Jamie Gaudette described Microsoft's challenge of growing infrastructure 10x over the next four years without increasing operational headcount, while managing one of the world's largest backbone networks, which recently surpassed one exabit per second of traffic.\n\nMicrosoft discovered that many operational bottlenecks were not technical configuration tasks, but rather the coordination of people, field services, carriers, and repair activities. AI agents proved particularly effective in these workflow-heavy scenarios.\n\nOne example is Miles, an AI agent responsible for coordinating the resolution of outside plant fiber cuts.       "content": "## Our approach\n\nKPMG in India designed and implemented an enterprise-wide digital transformation program focused on creating a unified digital core while delivering high-impact operational improvements across the business.\n\nThe transformation began with the establishment of an enterprise data platform capable of integrating information from ERP, SCADA, IoT devices, HR systems, energy analytics applications, and operational platforms into a single source of truth.\n\n##### KPMG in India’s approach included:\n\n###### Enterprise Data Foundation\n\nCentralised integration of operational, financial, asset, and workforce data\n\n###### AI-Powered Operations\n\nPredictive maintenance, fault detection, forecasting, and performance optimisation\n\n###### Workflow Automation [...] A leading renewable energy platform in India was rapidly expanding its solar, wind, and battery energy storage portfolio.       "url": "https://www.adp.com/spark/articles/2026/07/how-to-work-with-your-ai-what-to-consider-before-adding-ai-to-your-toolset.aspx",
      "title": "How to Work with Your AI: What to Consider Before Adding ...",
      "content": "As HR leaders we can drive the effectiveness of AI by:\n\nOffering literacy pathways not just to technical teams but to operations, service, implementation/onboarding, and frontline roles.\n\nFraming AI literacy as a career enabler, not a niche skill.\n\nTracking literacy metrics alongside adoption and value metrics.\n\nWhen we level the field, we make AI adoption inclusive, fair, and effective. This is what “human” means in a connected future: everyone empowered, everyone competent.\n\n## 4. Building employee trust in AI-powered work\n\nScale matters, but without trust, scaling AI becomes fragile. [...] For HR, that means the work is not just about moving fast, it’s about moving right by embedding transparency, dialogue, and accountability in the introduction and use of AI. This means informing employees about what data is used and why, how the tools work, and how to consider both the benefits and the risks of using them.\n\nTrust also requires establishing human-in-the-loop checkpoints for use cases where there are matters at stake that affect people in significant ways. For HR, that's most of what we do.\n\nWhen HR frames AI with purpose, the conversation shifts from “We built it” to “We built it together with trust, clarity, and human intent.” That is what being human means in the AI era.\n\n## How to prepare your organization for AI success [...] Why is AI governance important?\n\nAI governance helps organizations manage risk, improve accountability, support compliance efforts, and ensure responsible use of AI systems.\n\nWhat is AI literacy?\n\nAI literacy refers to employees' ability to understand, use, evaluate, and safely interact with AI-powered tools.\n\nHow can HR teams build trust in AI?\n\nHR leaders can build trust through transparency, communication, human oversight, training, and clear governance policies.\n\nShould AI replace human decision-making?\n\nMost HR and workforce applications benefit from AI-supported decision-making combined with human review and accountability.\n\nTags\n\nSubscribe to SPARK updates\n\nStay in the know on the latest workforce trends and insights.\n\n## Recommended for You\n\n### Tools & Resources",

      "content": "Accenture\n\nCredit: HJBC / Shutterstock\n\nOne of the challenges of IT operations at a global consulting firm like Accenture is it runs a huge and diverse portfolio of technologies to drive its digital core. Maintaining and operating that core requires continuously developing deep skillsets that are becoming rarer as every industry competes within a limited talent pool.\n\nAccenture’s answer is the Accenture Advanced Technology Agent (AATA), an agentic AI-powered integration platform that sits between the company’s human workforce and its technology platforms, and something that’s earned the company a 2025 CIO 100 Award in IT Excellence. [...] To smooth that process, AATA is an agnostic, open system with agentic architecture that enables IT teams and end users to interact with the core to resolve issues or deliver customer solutions without having to connect to an agent or file a single ticket.\n\nAccenture started working on AATA in 2023, starting with a conceptual architectural model. “Then we started to think about how people would consume the technology to derive value, so we wanted it to be largely democratized,” Courtney says. “You could have an open standards orchestration layer and a consistent prompt layer, but then enable teams to be able to either consume natively available agents, plug in existing automation or gen AI processes, or actually create custom agents if that was what required.” [...] 1.       "url": "https://bankingblog.accenture.com/agentic-ai-future-of-work",
      "title": "Agentic AI and the future of work in financial services | Accenture Banking Blog",
      "content": "We developed AI agents to sit on top of the claims platform and orchestrate out to other systems, supporting the human claims handler. The AI agents support tasks such as information gathering, data quality, policy and coverage checks, policy detail extraction, claim data summarization (including the first notification of loss, customer and expert inputs, customer correspondence) and even some support to litigation, fraud and reserve management. [...] ### What is agentic architecture?\n\nAI agents are programs that handle tasks and workflows to achieve specific goals. Humans set the goals, but the agents operate more independently, adapting their strategies as needed to achieve the goal. They take inputs, reason, decide on tasks to perform, interact with other agents and tools, review their outcomes and determine the next steps required.\n\nThe agents ‘know’ a domain context in which they have been trained within an organization (e.g. on specific training data and documents). They have long-term memory and can learn from past interactions to optimize decision-making. [...] Through all these tasks the agents support the claims handler to be in charge as the ‘human in the lead’ — for instance, they can look back into source data easily. We have been able to free up 20% of their capacity, focusing their time on better decision-making (improving claims accuracy by 1%) and supporting negotiation in the most complex and valuable claims.\n\nWe’ve seen similar work from a US-based P&C insurer through to complex commercial claims operations.\n\n### The ‘so what’ for work and workforce\n\nImagine agentic AI as your co-worker, where you have team members dedicated to you who specialize in their support to you and can even bring perspectives and strengths complementary to your own.",

      "title": "Neue Chancen und Aufgaben für HR durch Agentic AI | Deloitte Deutschland",
      "content": "Agentic AI kombiniert die Fähigkeiten von Generativer KI (GenAI) mit intelligenten Agenten, die in der Lage sind, kontextbezogen zu planen, Daten zu integrieren und Workflows zu orchestrieren. Diese Technologie ermöglicht es, Routineaufgaben zu automatisieren, komplexe Prozesse zu optimieren und personalisierte Erlebnisse für Mitarbeiter zu schaffen.\n\n#### Systemische Co-Dependenz\n\nIn einer Agentic-AI-Welt kann kein Unternehmensbereich isoliert agieren – weder Technologie, Operations, Talent, Customer, Finance, Risk noch Legal. Es braucht systemische Co-Dependenz, bei der Fortschritt nur durch gemeinsame Verantwortung und abgestimmte Ausrichtung möglich ist.\n\n#### Drei zentrale Handlungsfelder für die Zukunft [...] #### Die Zukunft des Personalmanagements\n\nDie Einführung von Agentic AI erfordert Investitionen in digitale Technologien, die Umgestaltung von Arbeitsprozessen und die Weiterentwicklung menschlicher Fähigkeiten wie kritisches Denken und emotionale Intelligenz. Unternehmen, die diese Transformation aktiv gestalten, können HR zu einem strategischen Partner machen, der nicht nur Kosten senkt, sondern auch Innovation und Wachstum fördert, indem er den Übergang zu einer kombinierten Belegschaft aus Mitarbeitenden und KI-Agenten vorantreibt.\n\nFür die Weiterentwicklung des HR-Bereichs sind unterschiedliche Szenarien denkbar, die sich durch den Grad der Integration von Agentic AI und die strategische Ausrichtung der HR-Funktion unterscheiden: [...] #### Drei zentrale Handlungsfelder für die Zukunft\n\nDiese drei Imperative sind nicht sequenziell, sondern voneinander abhängig.       "url": "https://www.deloitte.com/lu/en/our-thinking/future-of-advice/hr-to-lead-agentic-ai.html",
      "title": "From tool-mate to teammate: How HR has to lead the rise of Agentic AI | Deloitte Luxembourg | Future of Advice",
      "content": "Think of it this way: Traditional AI is the assistant waiting for your next command. Agentic AI is the teammate who flags problems before they escalate and suggests next steps you might not have seen. Like any new team member, it needs onboarding. Done right, it becomes a trusted partner that manages operational tasks, surfaces new insights, or alerts you when something’s off.\n\nNearly nine in ten HR professionals using AI in recruiting say it saves time, and more than one in three reports reduced hiring costs2. Agentic AI is already being piloted across HR, finance, technology, and other support functions. We’ve seen AI agents draft onboarding plans, schedule interviews, and even detect early signs of burnout based on behavioral signals. This evolution is well underway. [...] This article explores how Agentic AI is transforming organizations, and why HR must take the lead. The central questions are: Are HR professionals ready to work alongside AI agents? And what kind of collaborators do we want them to be?\n\n#### What is Agentic AI and why does it matter?\n\nChances are, you already use AI every day, through tools like ChatGPT, automated workflows, or recommendation engine. Agentic AI takes it further, designed from the start by HR’s scope, priorities, and values. Unlike traditional AI, which waits for instructions, agentic systems can act, choosing when and how to execute tasks. [...] #### Conclusion\n\nAgentic AI isn’t a side experiment or an upgrade in automation. It’s your next generation of talent. And like any new generation, it brings new ways of working, new expectations, and a lot of potential.The real challenge isn’t adoption; it’s building the structures that let your organization manage AI agents effectively and capture their full value.This is about people, process, and performance, not just tools. Developing capability in prompting, data judgment, and oversight is a need as these will define who thrives in this new landscape and who gets left behind.\n\nSo go check in on Eli.       "title": "ServiceNow and agentic AI future | Deloitte Insights",
      "content": "One especially powerful use case he’s seeing is new-employee onboarding. Every new hire needs access to human resources systems as well as tools and data specific to their role. In the past, new workers would engage with a range of helpdesk workers, retrieve passwords, log into different systems, and assemble the credentials they needed to start doing their job. Now, AI enables the HR systems to learn more quickly what new hires need and automatically provision access by the respective employee’s start date. [...] These domain-specific agents could be an upgrade over existing robotic process automation tools, which do some of the same things but are also brittle and can’t adapt to changing environments. Domain-specific agents will be better at proactive execution, for example, seeing that a business has a new employee onboarding next week and automatically provisioning the employee’s access to facilities, entering them into payroll systems, scheduling their training, and executing across all the necessary areas.\n\n“That’s where things are heading,” Bedi says. “We’re already seeing glimpses of it. Agentic [AI] answers the question of how we actually get work done.”4 [...] Enterprise information technology is regularly upended by emerging technologies that force a rethink of how work gets done. Past examples are client server, cloud, and mobile. Today, agentic artificial intelligence is causing a shift in how technology teams—and the business units they support—operate.       "title": "Agentic Enterprise: AI treibt digitale Transformation | EY - Deutschland",
      "content": "Die Umsetzung von Agentic AI erfolgt entlang Ihrer bestehenden Unternehmensprozesse – von Finance über HR bis hin zu Supply Chain und Marketing. Intelligente Agenten übernehmen Aufgaben, treffen Entscheidungen und interagieren mit anderen Agenten und Mitarbeitenden. Das Agentic Enterprise Framework definiert klare Rollen: Orchestrator Agents koordinieren, Expert Agents führen aus, Ecosystem Agents sichern Governance und Compliance. Unsere strategischen Allianzen mit führenden Technologieanbietern ermöglichen eine nahtlose Integration in Ihre Systemlandschaft. Gemeinsam schaffen wir eine skalierbare, transparente und leistungsfähige Plattform für Ihre Agentic Enterprise Transformation. [...] Im Rahmen des Agentic Enterprise Framework übernehmen HR Agents unterschiedliche Rollen – als Orchestratoren, Analytiker und Gestalter einer verbesserten Employee Experience. Dabei können bestehende HR-Systeme wie SuccessFactors oder ServiceNow gezielt um KI-Funktionalitäten erweitert werden. Gleichzeitig lassen sich neue Agenten nahtlos in die bestehende HR-Landschaft integrieren, um Synergien zu schaffen und Prozesse intelligent zu vernetzen.\n\nDoch Technologie allein reicht nicht: Die Einführung neuer KI-Lösungen erfordert ein durchdachtes Change-Management, das Mitarbeitende mitnimmt, Akzeptanz schafft und Vertrauen fördert. So wird HR nicht nur effizienter, sondern zum strategischen Partner, der proaktiv die Zukunft der Arbeit gestaltet.\n\n## Ihr Ansprechpartner [...] Agentic AI ist mehr als ein technologischer Trend – es ist ein strategischer Imperativ. Unternehmen stehen vor der Herausforderung, steigende Komplexität, Fachkräftemangel und wachsende Erwartungen an Geschwindigkeit und Personalisierung zu bewältigen. Agentic AI bietet eine Lösung: Durch autonome, lernfähige Agenten lassen sich Prozesse nicht nur effizienter gestalten, sondern auch völlig neu denken. Studien zeigen, dass bis zu 50 Prozent der administrativen Aufgaben automatisiert werden können – mit signifikanten Einsparungen und Produktivitätsgewinnen. Der Hebel in den wertschöpfenden Funktionen ist signifikant – in Produktions-, Logistik- und Sales-Prozesse integrierte Agentic AI bietet darüber hinaus ein großes Potenzial, Produkte erfolgreicher und schneller in die Märkte zu bringen.",

      "title": "Accelerating agentic AI deployment at a top pharmaceutical company | McKinsey",
      "content": "Accelerating agentic AI deployment at a top pharmaceutical company | McKinsey. Accelerating agentic AI deployment at a top pharmaceutical company. # Accelerating agentic AI deployment at a top pharmaceutical company. How we accelerated agentic AI POCs for specific domains to prepare for enterprise-wide transformation. McKinsey leveraged agentic AI to enhance productivity, efficiency, and customer satisfaction across sales and service divisions to scale for organizational transformation. ### The challenge. The client faced inefficiencies in market access operations due to manual processes, siloed data, and decentralized insight. The market access operations team had deployed limited AI use cases compared to other commercial sub-domains. The client identified AI agents as enablers to empower teams to focus on higher-value work and handle increased workloads. Accelerating agentic AI deployment at a top pharmaceutical company. ### The solution. Collaborating with Microsoft, McKinsey helped the client quickly develop agentic AI POCs to streamline market access operations. McKinsey also conducted an art of the possible gen AI/agentic AI workshop with clients to identify 14 core use cases to address. Based on this, the team developed a 12- to 18-month phased deployment approach based on priority use cases, starting with building and testing POCs to accelerate output. The effort then progressed to a 6-month MVP build of targeted areas to expand knowledge and conduct a “big bang” style launch. ### The result. McKinsey and Microsoft successfully deployed a Microsoft Copilot solution to deliver insights and support Commercial Sales in pre-call planning, which resulted in a 1–2 percent revenue increase. McKinsey also developed an integrated AI-enabled platform to review and correct Commercial Marketing content that led to a 5–20 percent reduction in content costs and streamline time to launch to 1–2 weeks.",

AI in Asia: Reimagining banking operations through agentic AI. # AI in Asia: Reimagining banking operations through agentic AI. Multiagentic systems are transforming operations, combining the power of technology, processes, and people to deliver outsized impact for banks in Asia. **Agentic AI is expected to have a transformative impact** on banking operations over the next decade, and many banking leaders are now seeking clarity on how AI and agentic AI can be harnessed in operations to optimize workflows, delight customers, cut costs, and increase productivity. This report is a collaborative effort by Abhilash Sridharan, Azam Mohammad, David Deninzon, Jan Henrich, Martin Rosendahl, Renny Thomas, Senthil Muthiah, Vinayak HV, and Violet Chung, with Hannes Bergström, Mint Namasondhi, Paras Chhabra, Rasika Ramesh, and Yuvika Motwani, representing views from McKinsey’s Operations Practice. Unlike previous technology waves, however, success with agentic AI and multiagentic systems will require an organization-level mindset shift and a fundamental rewiring of the way work gets done, and by whom.1*Seizing the agentic AI advantage*, QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey, June 13, 2025. McKinsey research highlights ten key domains within banking operations that offer significant opportunity for reimagination, especially when approached holistically and through a fleet of nine enhanced agentic AI ‘operations transformers’ (Exhibit 1). Against a backdrop of rising customer expectations and a challenging operating environment, three drivers help illustrate AI’s potential in banking operations:. **AI is expected to disrupt the operations function more than any other lever.** With end-to-end operations representing an estimated 60 to 70 percent of a bank’s cost base, based on McKinsey’s research and engagements, transforming operational processes could be an unprecedented value unlock in the financial services sector. Banks today have an immediate opportunity to harness agentic AI to fundamentally transform their operations. Ultimately, any undertaking to reimagine banking operations through AI is not simply a technology program; it is a strategic reinvention and rewiring of workflows.       "content": "The future of agentic AI in travel and hospitality | McKinsey. # Remapping travel with agentic AI. Agentic AI could upend the travel industry. Given the tremendous potential of agentic AI, travel and hospitality companies are beginning to experiment with it. What does the travel industry need to know as it ponders going all in on agentic AI? A new report, *Remapping travel with agentic AI*—a collaboration between McKinsey and Skift—examines the potential for agentic AI to unleash the full value of AI in travel. Based on analysis incorporating surveys of 1,002 travelers and 86 travel executives, the report traces the digital prologue that brought the industry to this moment, details agentic AI’s transformative capabilities for both travelers and travel companies, and provides a blueprint for travel and hospitality leaders who are eager to accelerate their organizations’ agentic AI initiatives. In a survey of 86 mostly US-based travel executives conducted for this report, 26 percent of respondents say that introducing AI to their organizations has led to cost reductions in operations, 30 percent say that it’s aiding faster decision-making, 33 percent say that it’s improving customer personalization, 36 percent say that it’s enabling higher-quality outputs, and 59 percent say that it’s increasing employee productivity. Perhaps chief among these is the advent of agentic AI, a cutting-edge technology poised to revolutionize the travel industry. ## The agentic-AI-powered future of customer experience in travel. ## How agentic AI can improve travel’s internal workflows. ### Agentic AI’s value for frontline travel workers. Of the travel executives we surveyed, 90 percent say that their organizations currently use gen AI in some capacity, but 38 percent say that they’re not using agentic AI at all. Insights and lessons learned from tech adoption efforts across various industries can provide a valuable road map for travel companies that hope to initiate or accelerate their own adoption of agentic AI.       "content": "## How will agentic AI impact the workforce?\n\n Productivity increases.People become AI supervisors rather than task executors.\n Roles shift.Agents democratize technical skills, increasing the breadth of employee roles.\n Decision making is redefined.Employee autonomy increases and decision cycles speed up.\n Collaboration becomes critical.Agents expedite work, but it remains important to coordinate interactions among people.\n Risk management expands.AI agents increase risk of unintended consequences, requiring new guardrails.\n\n## What should businesses do to prepare for agentic AI? [...] ## What barriers are hindering the adoption of agentic AI?\n\n Generalization beyond narrow scopes: AI agents perform well in tightly defined workflows, less so in complex contexts.\n Explanation of decisions: Agents are often “black boxes,” making it hard to validate decisions or fix errors.\n Workflow training:If workflows are undocumented, agents are limited to information at hand to operate independently.\n Cooperation among agents: Agents struggle to operate together without mature orchestration, architectures, and coordination.\n Data and tooling: Agents cannot act without access to clean data and integrated tooling.\n\n## How will agentic AI impact the workforce? [...] ## What should businesses do to prepare for agentic AI?\n\n Embed agents where ROI is greatest. Identify where vendor ecosystems, agentic AI technology, and your business intersect.\n Pilot fast, iterate faster. The agentic phase is moving faster than previous AI waves; test and iterate faster.\n Prepare data and tools. Set up agents for success so they can be rapidly adopted by your employees.\n Be wary of standalone platforms.Pressure test agents’ connectors to other systems.\n Become a learning organization.
